newsitem.title: UK: EBRD pledges more to former Soviet Union countries.
newsitem.headline: EBRD pledges more to former Soviet Union countries.

text.p: The European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD), set up five years ago to help the old East Bloc switch to capitalism, said on Thursday it was committing more funds to countries in the former Soviet Union.
"In the countries in the early stages of transition ...(commitments) have increased a lot," vice president for finance, Bart le Blanc, told reporters.
In its early years, nearly all of the EBRD's activities were focused on a few central Euopean countries.
But in the first six months of this year, half of its total commitments were to the former Soviet Union, and 50 percent of that to Russia alone.
The bank signed 33 projects in the first half of this year worth 774 million Ecu ($986.1 million) and up a third from the same period last year.

Le Blanc expected the EBRD to about break even this year after showing a modest first half net profit of 0.16 million Ecu ($203,800), adding the bank was doing as much as it could to build up provisions for possible future losses.
Banking operations contributed almost 40 percent to gross income, compared with 29 percent a year earlier.
Le Blanc said the bank, which has long cast off its early image of extravagence, would stick to its conservative approach, making sure it had enough funds to cover any losses and to keep costs low.

"Prudent financial management gives priority to building up the EBRD's reserves. Growth in operating income and continued cost control allows the bank to allocate significant amounts to provisions for unforeseen risks in the portfolio," he said.
About 70 percent of the bank's operations are in the private sector.
The bank would also continue to be active in raising funds in capital markets.

It has already issued bonds in central European countries and is now looking at a possible issue in the Baltics. It is also planning a South Korean won bond and considering one in Taiwan if it can sort out tax issues.

The bank could borrow up to another 250 million Ecu ($318.5 million) the rest of this year, but le Blanc said the EBRD's had enough liquidity of its own to mean it was not forced to go to the markets to borrow.
